utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Gustafson, are you ready to continue your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then may the witness be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just before the witness takes the stand. With respect to the Chamber's invitation last Friday, in -- concerning the Limaj and Popovic precedents, we have had a chance to review it in more detail over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not only -- I just gave by way of example --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Limaj, and there are more as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was trying to just keep it general so that the Chamber knew what I was referring to. We are prepared to address the issue in any manner that the Chamber wishes it be addressed, just so that the Chamber is aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to hear from the other parties once they are ready so that we can make it a focussed joint effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you have given at the beginning of your testimony. That may be clear to you. Ms. Gustafson will now continue her cross-examination. Ms. Gustafson, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now on Friday at the -- near the end of the court session, I was asking some questions about the military police in Knin, and you explained that you did not recall Mr. Dzolic, the first military police commander in Knin, and explained that you were not present at any meetings between General Cermak and the military police. Now, in your statement that you gave to the Defence, you stated that the military police was not subordinate to General Cermak. And I'd like to ask you if you're aware that General Cermak issued written orders to the military police commander in Knin. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that. I told you last time that members of the military police did not participate in meetings together with me and Mr. Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I -- it's clear from your statement that you know that General Cermak was the garrison commander in Knin. Do have you any specialised knowledge about the authority or function of a garrison commander under the rules and laws that applied at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, a garrison commander does not have any special authorities, save for supplying units currently deployed in the territory of the town where that person serves as a garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you aware of -- of which particular rules and laws applied to define the functions and authority of a garrison commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to information available to me, I believe that those tasks belong to the civilian sector. They certainly did not belong or fall within the purview of either the military or the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that you are not aware of which particular rules and laws applied to define the functions and authority of a garrison commander at the time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I don't think you're right. His authorities fell within the purview of the civilian sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, my question was about particular laws or rules that applied at the time. Are you able to identify any particular law or rule that applied at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I must say, unfortunately, that I don't understand your question. What laws and rules? The laws and rules of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your statement that you gave to the Prosecution, you explained that General Cermak was upset about the crimes that were going on after Operation Storm. You stated: "As far as the killings, looting, and destruction was concerned, he was not happy about it." And in your statement to the Defence, you stated that General Cermak did not have the authority that would allow him to prevent crime. Now, as far as you were aware, did General Cermak have the authority to instruct either the military police or the civilian police to take action in response to the report of a crime, to investigate a crime. Did he have that authority, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not have that authority. And as a person who was serving as the garrison commander and as the person who cooperated with me, I told you that he felt upset after having received reports about lootings and killings and other such things.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So I take it that you are not aware of any specific instance where General Cermak instructed either the civilian police or the military police to -- to respond to a crime or to investigate a crime; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, in your statement that you gave to the Defence, you describe an incident where you invited General Cermak to your village and that General Cermak organised a delivery of a generator and fuel to the village. And that's at paragraph 30 of your Defence statement. Now, your village is -- you have described as Oton. Are you actually from the hamlet of Oton Bender? Is that right? I see you nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like, if we could have P2526, page 82 of the English and page 98 of the B/C/S on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, the document that's going to appear on your screen shortly is part of an interview that General Cermak gave to the Prosecution, and I'm going to ask you to read some parts of that interview and then ask you a couple of questions, okay? And the passage I'd like to you look at begins in the first paragraph where General Cermak is speaking, and he says: "Just before winter, in October, I was with my people from logistics. We went to the Serbian village of Bender, that's near Knin, because I wanted in the villages surrounding Knin where there were people of Serbian nationality, the people who stayed had behind, that in each village there would be an electricity generator. So I went with my logistics people, and also with the government representative, Mr. Pasic" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, is it --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for certain that we have the version in the language of the witness on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think so. I think at this point we're in the paragraph in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I see, as a matter of fact, on my screen is that in the middle we have a relatively short paragraph, whereas you apparently are reading from a paragraph which covers some 26 lines, and I do not see --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- any beginning, unless it is the very last one, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think it actually is broken up. I believe this is one of the places where there's an interjection by Mr. Dondo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That could be, and -- yes, if that is the case, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Are you able to follow so far, Mr. Pasic? If you could look at this point at the paragraph in the middle. And I'll just repeat. General Cermak says -- he mentions your name and then he says: "I went to that village. We set up the generator. We connected the electricity to the village, delivered humanitarian aid. We delivered a couple of televisions so that they wouldn't be cut off from the world and could watch the news. So we talked with people and they roasted lamb for us. We said good-bye. We gave somebody from the village the responsibility to maintain and to fix the generator, and we set off back for Knin." And now, just stopping there for a moment. The incident that General Cermak is describing there, as far as you are aware, is that the same one that you mentioned in your witness statement, where you said that you invited General Cermak to your native village and he organised the delivery of a generator to your village? Is that the same thing that General Cermak talks about here?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my screen I don't see written what you have just quoted, but can I say with certainty that there were no incidents. We went there together, and everything corresponds in terms of the contents. We brought the generator, we established the delivery of electricity, humanitarian aid was brought, we spoke to people because we wanted for the people who remained behind and were scared to gain trust in the Croatian authorities, and to make sure that they understand that they would receive as much help and aid as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could move down to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if could you look at that last paragraph, Mr. Pasic. And in the English, General Cermak says: "As soon as I arrived at the office, I received a report that in the village three or four people had arrived with a truck. They took sheep away from the people. They put them in the truck."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could move to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, can I see that, and it is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we -- if you look at the first large paragraph on your screen, he continues: "They took the televisions that we had given to them" -- sorry. "They took sheep away from the people. They put them in the truck. They took the televisions that we had given to them and I was just completely angry. I exploded. I called the civilian police commander. That was the one who came after Romanic, a Mr. Gambiroza. Do whatever you want, I want the culprits to be found. And I got everyone going. Two or three hours went by and the culprits were captured. One policeman, a civilian policeman with his badge, with his identification. Another policeman who had been suspended a couple of months before, and another two civilians." I take it from your previous answer that you know that the villagers were robbed immediately after your and General Cermak's visit to the village. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just one isolated case, which happened --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'm just asking if you know about it. Do you know? Did you know that the villagers were robbed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not robbed. It was not villagers but a villager who was robbed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you know that immediately after General Cermak found out about this robbery that he called Mr. Gambiroza, told him to do whatever he wanted, he wanted the culprits to be found, and that General Cermak got everyone going. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed General Cermak about the incident. It was a robbery that was perpetrated against my uncle, a man that I shared my residence with, and General Cermak reacted in the way he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was just asking if you knew about that reaction. Did you know about General Cermak's phone call to Mr. Gambiroza and what he said to Mr. Gambiroza?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 1802, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pasic, your uncle who was robbed, is his name Luka Pasic; is that right. Oh. Mr. Pasic, is your uncle that was robbed, is his name Luka Pasic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, on your screen --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could scroll down in the English. I think that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You can see this is a report from the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we move up in the B/C/S, you can see it's from the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And it's addressed to a number of recipients, including General Cermak, and the subject is plaintiff, Luka Pasic, criminal act of aggravated theft. And if could you read the text near the bottom of the page, you can see this describes an incident in the village of Oton Bender on the 19th of October, 1995, related to a criminal act by three unidentified perpetrators who took away 56 heads of sheep. And it describes how three suspects have been detained. When you get to the bottom of the page, we can turn to the next page in the B/C/S, as it continues. And the report describes how the suspects were brought to the Knin police station. Describes how one of the suspects was a MUP employee, and another had been removed six months earlier as a MUP employee. And can you see that the report --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we go to the last page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- is written by Mr. Gambiroza. Now, it appears from reading this report that it deals with the same incident of theft that you describe in your -- that you've just described and that General Cermak described in his interview. Is this, again, dealing with the same incident?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive this document, but I believe that it speaks about the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You -- now, having seen this evidence of General Cermak learning about a crime, calling the police commander, Mr. Gambiroza, telling him to do whatever he wants, he wants the perpetrators found, getting everyone going, and having seen this report from Mr. Gambiroza back to General Cermak reporting on the results of the investigation, is it fair to say that when you gave your statements you were not aware of the full extent of General Cermak's authority, in relation to the investigation of crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before the witness answers the question and in the need for fullness if he is being asked to comment on it, my learned friend should put the following document, 65 ter 2D0005, which is the original report from Luka Pasic to the police and has details there, which is a document that has to be considered in this context.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not familiar with that document. If -- I think the question is a fair one but if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither is --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- I would need time to read the document to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither is the Court, Ms. Gustafson. So, therefore, although I understand the words of Mr. Kay to be a suggestion, but a suggestion of a kind which should be seriously considered. I'm not saying whether finally if you would have looked at the document, whether it would be appropriate to ask you to include this information but at least I can't, at this moment, say anything about it. But would be please be so kind to have a look at it and see whether ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. It's the criminal report to the police on -- by Luka Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I put 2D305 into e-court I don't get any result. Perhaps it's another number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, sorry, it's four zeros.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: 2D300005, I still get no document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 2D00005. I'm sorry for the confusion but that is it the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we have -- I did understand 2D300 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: There's no 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, 3, Your Honour. Forget the 3. It's 2D00005. And forget the 4 as a digit. It's just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I now repeat, 2D00005.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have looked at the document. I could respond, but perhaps the witness should take his headphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you take your earphones off, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: From what I can see, Your Honour, this is a criminal report by the plaintiff, Mr. Luka Pasic, to the Knin police. I don't see how this impacts on what the witness has seen or the question. The evidence that Mr. Pasic might have made a report to the Knin police station, I don't think, impacts on the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it, Ms. Gustafson, that the issue Mr. Kay is raising is that it may have been the reporting by Mr. Pasic himself that triggered the police activity, rather than a phone call on which -- phone call which is mentioned in Mr. Cermak's statement. Now, whether this should be put to him or not, of course, the first thing before we ask any conclusions as to the authority of Mr. Cermak, the witness has testified that he was not aware of what may have been said during this telephone conversation with Mr. Gambiroza. So perhaps we first establish what the witness knows, because there seems to be a statement in which Mr. Cermak refers to a telephone conversation he made. And what you're doing, actually, is looking at what then happened, and I take it that Mr. Kay is very much concerned about the solidity of the causal relationship between either Mr. Cermak calling Mr. Gambiroza or Mr. Pasic reporting a crime which may have triggered the police activity. Now, that is, certainly before we start drawing any conclusions as to the authority of Mr. Cermak, seems to be a matter which deserves proper attention. And if you say, well, you do not see how this in any way affects the knowledge - and that's what you said before - you can't see, you said, how this impacts on what the witness has seen or the question. The question was -- let me ... The question was is it -- you put to him the events; that is, Mr. Cermak calling the police commander, saying what he -- you have seen this evidence, phone call, Mr. Cermak telling them to do whatever he wants them to do and having seen this report from Mr. Gambiroza back to General Cermak reporting on the results of the investigation, is it fair to say that when you gave your statements you were not aware of the full extent of General Cermak's authority, in relation to the investigation of crimes. Now, there's a lot of suggestion in there that what may have triggered what exactly. Perhaps we first seek clarification from the witness, whether he has any personal knowledge about what triggered the police activity. If not, then he has not been aware of what was said in the telephone conversation, he has no knowledge of how it was reported back, and he has no knowledge as to what triggered the police activity. Under those circumstances, to ask the witness about the authority of Mr. Cermak might be a bit seeking opinion rather than evidence a witness of fact could provide.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to add further to the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The witness has been referred to things that Mr. Cermak has said, of course, which he wasn't present at himself and doesn't know the basis of Mr. Cermak's knowledge. He is being asked to comment on it on a very important matter without having actually been shown what in law, as the Court has heard expert evidence, is the trigger event which is the Article 141 report of a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that's in the document, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just explore first what the witness knows for a fact, and then, if that is insufficient, even to form any opinion about the matter, then we should refrain from asking him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're with us again, Mr. Pasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, this report --

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This report from Mr. Gambiroza that's on your screen that you -- you said you'd never seen it before, do you know anything about the circumstances that caused Mr. Gambiroza to produce this report and send it to General Cermak and others?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Should it be how the crime was reported?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, "circumstances" is a rather general question, and let's first hear the answer of the witness and then see whether we have to further explore. Do you know anything about the circumstances which caused this report to be produced and sent to the addressee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Luka Pasic reported a theft and the disappearance of his sheep. I was aware of that, and it was me who told him to go to the police to report the theft. As for any further progress of the investigation and the case itself, it's something that I'm not familiar with. This report by Mr. Gambiroza was not addressed to me. Therefore, I was not privy to the issue of investigation and potential finding of the property appropriated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said Mr. Luka Pasic reported a theft. Do you remember whether that was before you spoke to Mr. Cermak or after you spoke to Mr. Cermak, that -- that you told him to go to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before. Before the conversation with Mr. Cermak. I advised Mr. Cermak about the fact of my uncle's property going missing, only after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, please proceed. If you want to further explore the factual chronology, you're, of course, free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, just one clarification. You said -- you said before the conversation with Mr. Cermak. You -- I take it that you spoke with your uncle and you told him to report the crime to the police and then you spoke with General Cermak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how long was it between the time you spoke to your uncle and the time you spoke to General Cermak? A couple of minutes, a couple of hours, a couple of days? How much time passed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few hours, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And after you spoke to your uncle and told him to report the crime to the police, do you know when precisely he actually went to the police and reported that crime?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't -- I went to see my uncle in his village, and I took him to the police station, to report the property gone missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when was that -- how long was that after you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, with the uncle?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You said you spoke with him and told him to report the crime to the police. And then you said you went to see him in his village and took him to the police station. After you spoke with him and told him to report the crime, how much time passed until you went to the village and took him to the police station? Was the same day, the next day, the day after?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you remember now approximately how many hours passed between when you spoke with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall that I was in my uncle's house, and he was supposed to bring the sheep back that afternoon. He went to fetch them and found them gone. I suppose it was around 5.00 or 5.30, perhaps 6.00 p.m. I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you -- when you took your uncle to the police station, was that before or after you had told General Cermak about the crime?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sure. You -- as I understand it, all in the same day, your uncle told you about the crime. You told General Cermak about the crime. And you took your uncle to the police station. Did you take your uncle to the police station before or after you told General Cermak about the crime?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took my uncle to the police station before that and then I advised Mr. Cermak of the incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, could 2D00005 be made an exhibit whilst we're on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour, and I thank you for the reminder that I would like to tender 65 ter 1802.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, may I take it, Mr. Kay suggested that you would look at 2D00005, then it's not entirely clear to me whether Mr. Kay also suggested that you would tender that document. I'm just considering whether or not it will be a Prosecution or a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: From my perspective, Your Honour, I'm not sure it matters very much. I'm not sure what my friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, nevertheless I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps keep them together as a P number if that assists. If my learned friend doesn't have an objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, they're -- I actually think they're distinct documents perhaps they need to be given two numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that it would be wiser to have two exhibit numbers. Mr. Registrar, doesn't make that much of a difference but could we have two P numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 65 ter 1802 becomes Exhibit P2645; and 2D00005 becomes Exhibit P2646.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And both are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'd like to turn another subject now. You explained in your statement to the Defence that after you arrived in Knin, you described your first meeting with General Cermak, and you said: "The objective of the first meeting with General Cermak was to protect property and facilitate an organised return to Knin of the Croats who had been living in hotels. The Knin garrison command issued blank passes which General Cermak gave to me. I gave them to Croats who were accommodated in hotels in Sibenik and Primosten."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could have D489 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, you can see this is a certificate confirming that you -- it's dated the 9th of August. It confirms that you took up passes for entering into the Knin garrison, and it says it's delivered by General Cermak. And my question is: You describe in your statement the Knin garrison command issuing blank passes which General Cermak gave to you. Is this certificate relate to the same thing you describe in your statement; namely, General Cermak issuing these passes to you for people to enter Knin? If you look on the screen to the document.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, when General Cermak issued these passes and gave them to you, did he give you any instructions as to how you should hand out these passes, to whom you should give them? What did he say to you when he gave you these passes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As he was handing the passes over, he didn't tell me anything. According -- according to the needs of those who came into the office that was in Sibenik, a selection was made; that is to say, the office distributed those passes which we had received from General Cermak, that is to say, the garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Did he give you these passes in person?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I am Petar Pasic, but the passes were received by another person, the person who actually received them signed it. It is Zikica Bunac [phoen], and that is not myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we look at D491, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is a document dated the 11th of August, addressed to General Cermak, and the subject is the list of issued passes delivered.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You can see that it is signed by you. Now, this document appears to reflect you reporting back to General Cermak with a list of individuals to whom passes were issued; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a facsimile of my signature. It is my signature, indeed, and I think the contents are true.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, did General Cermak have the authority to issue these passes that you gave out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had the authority. But if I may add, these passes were a positive development because, in that way --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pasic. I'm not seeking your opinion on the passes at the moment. Let me ask you this: You -- General Cermak gave you the passes, you handed them out, you reported back to him on -- as to who they were issued to. Was there anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He didn't say about reporting back. That was not the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You sent this document back to General Cermak identifying the persons to whom passes were issued. Was there anything that caused to you question or doubt General Cermak's authority to issue these passes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no doubts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move to Exhibit D422, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, in your statement to the Prosecution, you said that: "The Serbs who left their homes during Oluja were required to make a request to return to them by a date in December 1995. If they failed to do so, their home became the property of the state. This does not apply now, as the law has been changed."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move to the next page in the B/C/S, please. Actually, in the B/C/S, it's the law that begins at the bottom of the first column.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, this is the Law on Temporary Taking Over and Administration of Specified Property, dated the 20th of September, 1995. Is this the law that you were referring to in your Prosecution statement?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could move to Article 3 of this law.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is the Article that describes the property covered by this law, and it says: "Property under this law shall be considered any movable and immovable property ..." And then it goes into more detail and onto the next page in the English. Now, on Thursday, you were asked a question by the Presiding Judge about why people returning from Serbia could not regain possession of their furniture from the new tenants and your answer referred to a decision of the government. And my question is: Is this what you're referring to here, this provision of the Law on the Temporary Take Over of Property which includes under that law, furniture. Is that what you were talking about when you spoke about a decision of the government?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could move to Article 11 of this law, which is on the fourth page in the English and the next page of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, on -- on Thursday, you also said that people who had --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: May I ask that the witness take his earphones off again, please. Just if we could establish some foundation with this witness. I know he was on the ground. I don't know if he's familiar or how familiar he is with these laws, but my recollection of the discussion on Friday had to do with socially owned flats as opposed to the temporary take over of property. As counsel knows, there were two separate sets of laws I believe which the Gotovina Defence has now bar tabled. One which deal with the issue of socially owned flats; another which deals property, personal property or real property owned by other individuals. And just so that we don't mix up what the witness said Thursday concerning socially owned flats and then whether the Law on Temporary Take Over applies to socially owned flats as well, if we could just get some foundation from the witness as to what he knows about that and whether he believes that this law applied to socially owned flats as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you referred to -- I think to questions that were put by me, and it is my recollection that was specifically focussing on socially owned flats which would then be given to other persons and then I said something about the furniture.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, the Your Honour, in his evidence, I think suggested that all property was socially owned, and then he referred to this decision about furniture. This is the only provision that I could identify that referred to furniture. I wanted to clarify what the witness was talking about. In relation to Mr. Misetic's point, the witness has made a very clear statement in his Prosecution statement about Serbs leaving their homes being required to make a request to return, and if they failed to do so, their home became the property of the state. That doesn't refer to socially owned property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to keep matters -- I wouldn't say simple but at least clear. It's not my recollection, but please point me to the point where the witness said that all property was socially owned, and it certainly does not fit within evidence we received -- all of the evidence we received on the matter. Clearly he was talking at that moment about socially owned apartments. That's one. Now, you put the question to the witness in relation to what we discussed on Thursday, and if you say, This is the only legal provision I could find in relation to furniture, then that does not automatically link it to my question and the answer given to that. Ms. Gustafson, may I take it that you're now fully aware of the concerns of Mr. Misetic and you'll keep this in the back of your mind when formulating the question so as to avoid whatever misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm moving off that point and going back to what he said in his Prosecution statement, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we start with a kind of new entry of the subject. Please proceed. And could the witness put his earphones on again, yes. Please proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, in your Prosecution statement you said that Serbs who left were required to make a request to have their property returned to them by a date in December 1995. Now, in fact, in accordance with Article 11, Serbs actually had to return to Croatia in order to make that request; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. Some Serbs who were abroad could send, and did, a document through notary public about the protection of their property in Knin which means that Serbs residing in Republika Srpska and in the Republic of Serbia could also do the same and submit a document to protect their property.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you explain how that was possible, in accordance with this law, which states that if the owner of the property returns to the Republic of Croatia and claims this property for his restitution and you -- within 90 days, et cetera, "the Commission shall reverse the decision under Article 5 of this law."

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. If there were claims for property restitution, and as far as I can remember, there was a very low number of requests from abroad, there were no such requests, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you think requests were possible from abroad, but you can't remember any such requests; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were requests. I received them from London, from New York, from -- but I can't interpret this law. I suppose that one had to have a Croatian citizenship in order to claim property restitution. I suppose that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The requests that you received from abroad, were those requests from Serbs trying to regain their property, or were those requests from Croats who wanted to move and -- and have property in Croatia allocated to them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was about the protection of property of Knin citizens of both ethnic groups, Croats and Serbs alike.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just having trouble understanding your evidence because you said: "There was a very low number of requests from abroad, there were no such requests, as far as I can remember." And then a little later you said: "There were requests. I received from London, from New York ..."

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're talking about the citizens of Knin who had left the area before Operation Storm and had resided abroad for a long time and then sent in requests for protection of their property.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you receive any requests from abroad from any Croatian Serbs who had fled at the time of or after Operation Storm, who were residing in places like Bosnia, Serbia, or Hungary, to have their property returned to them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. But I would say that it is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move on to something else you said in your Prosecution statement, which was that you received instructions from Mr. Radic to house returning Croats in Knin and the surrounding villages. And you stated that Knin itself was soon very full. And that's at page 8 of your Prosecution statement. Now, this process of bringing Croats into Knin, you were not only returning Croats who had left Knin earlier, but you were also moving people in who were ethnic Croats from other places, such as Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Knin itself, it changed. The demographic picture in Knin changed substantially. In 1991, Knin had a large percentage -- a large majority of Serbs; and in the months after Operation Storm, that changed and it became a large majority of Croats. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, the population structure of Knin changed. 90 per cent of the population had been Serbs, and 8.3 per cent had been Croats. In 1991, only 250 Croats lived in Knin when Oluja started. In 1995, the situation was reversed. The Serbs left and the Croats returned and now this ratio was probably reversed. There was probably 90 per cent Croats and 8 to 9 per cent Serbs by that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could look at 65 ter 2D00054, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, if you look at the screen, you can see this is a document dated the 30th of August. It's addressed to you. It's from General Cermak. And it says: "Please find enclosed the letters of the citizens interested in living and working in Knin ..." And it lists the names of four people and says: "Since you are competent for acceptance of all returned displaced people and future workers interested in living and working in Knin, you should study seriously the aforementioned letters and facilitate solving citizens' requests ..." Now, this letter indicates that there are four ethnic Croats, Ivan Vujic, Nikola Dumandzic, and Marija and Miroslav Tomljanovic, who want to move to Knin. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say whether they are ethnic Croats or not just by their names and where they come from, but I will allow for that possibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now there are -- in addition to this letter, there are a number of other similar letters from General Cermak to you. Do you recall receiving such letters?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not so many from General Cermak as I did from Mr. Radic, from the county office.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And after receiving a letter like this, would you then work on finding housing for these people?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the commissioner's office of the Republic of Croatia for Knin we had a housing office which was composed of the officers of the commissioner's office, the Croatian Red Cross, members of the Ministry of Interior, I believe, and the Ministry of Defence. They were the ones who would determine priorities and who would also issue decisions for those who wanted to be provided with residences in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this -- one -- two of the names on this letter refer to Marija and Miroslav Tomljanovic, and it says "Germany." Is this a couple that live in Germany and want to move to Knin? Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names don't ring any bells. But judging by the letter, I would say that they, indeed, wanted to come back from Germany and start living in Croatia again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And was it the case that Croats from other countries were able to come to the Knin area and obtain housing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people, there were Croats from Canada, who also submitted a request for housing. I can tell you that I know of only one such case that was seen through. How many others there were, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how General Cermak came to have this list of names or these letters from people who wanted to move into Knin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that the senders of those letters misunderstood General's position. They probably thought that he was the one who could help them with their housing problems. He, in his turn, would refer all such letters to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document and there are five similar letters from General Cermak to Mr. Pasic that I would also like to tender. They're all on the Defence 65 ter list. The others are 2D00014, 2D00212, 2D00450, 2D00550, and 2D00691.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw that Mr. Kay was nodding that there no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, it might be useful here to take them as a batch together. Mr. Registrar, the documents just mentioned by Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this can be consolidated into one document, and it will be under 2D00054 and gets Exhibit P2647.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2647 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I'd like to move to another subject. You said in your testimony on Thursday, you said that, as far as you knew, there weren't any obstacles for those who were willing to return, who had expressed their wish to return, and this was given in the context of Croatian Serbs after Operation Storm. Now, it's the case, is it not, that, in the months after Operation Storm, there were thousands of Croatian Serb refugees trying to return to Croatia who were prevented from returning by the Croatian authorities. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to know the number of those who wanted to return. However, the Croatian government did not prevent the displaced Serbs from returning. Prior to doing that, they had to obtain Croatian documents, and the Croatian government made sure that the displaced Serbs obtained documents in Vukovar and Beli Manastir. And now, if you're looking at the matters, you can see that a number of Serbs who have returned in the meantime have documents that were issued by the offices in Beli Manastir and Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, I would like to read to you two paragraphs of a report from the UN Special Rapporteur for the former Yugoslavia, dated the 7th of November, 1995, Ms. Elisabeth Rehn. And the context of these paragraphs is her discussion of the Law on the Temporary Take Over of Property that we looked at a few moments ago. And on 7 November, she said --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the Court and the parties, this is P639, paragraphs 40 and 41.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: "Furthermore, the Special Rapporteur notes the difficulties facing refugees in returning to Croatia within the deadline in order to reclaim properties. The Croatian Office for Displaced Persons and Refugees has established a procedure for return. After studying the regulations, the Special Rapporteur is convinced that the vast majority of refugees, regardless of their own intentions, will not be able to meet these requirements. "During the meeting with the Special Rapporteur, the deputy prime minister, Mr. Ivica Kostovic, stated that all those who are able to present the required documents would be allowed to return. According to him, this proves the seriousness of the government in its officially proclaimed policy towards the return of refugees. However, the Special Rapporteur points out that a couple of thousand Croatian Serb refugees are already waiting in Hungary for return and are being prevented from doing so by various bureaucratic measures instituted by Croatian officials. "Reports have been received of various administrative obstacles and the very uncooperative attitude towards refugees of both the Croatian liaison office in Belgrade and the Croatia embassy in Budapest. Other reports confirm that refugees have been turned back at the border, despite being in possession of the necessary documentation, including Croatian citizenship papers. Given that return within the prescribed time-limits does not appear feasible, the requirement that the owners must be in Croatia constitutes an insurmountable obstacle for Serbs currently outside Croatia." Do you, Mr. Pasic, have any reason to question the observations of the Special Rapporteur as I read them out to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read and I heard that report, and I believe that I reacted to Mrs. Rehn's report, and I did not agree with her report. I cannot question the words of Mrs. Rehn, but I also can't question the words of my deputy prime minister, Mr. Kostovic. So there's no way I can believe the words of Mrs. Rehn and not believe the words of my government official.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 2353, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, this is a -- what's about to come on your screen is a memo from Mr. Al-Alfi, dated the 12th of October, 1995. And you were shown, on Thursday, I believe, another memo by Mr. Al-Alfi, and I believe you mentioned that you remembered Mr. Al-Alfi. Is that right? I see you're nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the title of this document is: Meeting with the mayor of Knin. Now, Mr. Pasic -- and if you go to the first paragraph, he is describing a meeting that he with you on the 12th of October in Knin. Do you remember now --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, if we could go to the previous page in the B/C/S. Oh, sorry, no. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you remember now meeting with Mr. Al-Alfi on the 12th of October, Mr. Pasic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 2 in the English and stay on page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Pasic, I'd like to direct your attention to point 5, which is at the bottom of the page. And it says: "According to the mayor, the Croatian Office of Displaced Persons is preparing a list of those who want to leave the area. He expressed disagreement with such an approach. On the contrary, in his opinion, those who left the area should be encouraged to return. He went further to express his disagreement with the policy regarding the return of those who left the area as expressed recently by Mr. Kostovic, deputy prime minister."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go down to point 7, which is on the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It says: "From the meeting, I could sense that the mayor reached a point of frustration and he hinted that there is a possibility he may be changed very soon. It may be recalled that the mayor is of Serb origin and he is from this area. He informed me that it is very difficult for him to continue holding this post of mayor of Knin at a time when this area turned to be purely an area for Croats." Now, do you recall saying this to Mr. Al-Alfi, that you disagreed with the policy regarding the return of those who left the area, as expressed recently by the deputy prime minister, Mr. Kostovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with this statement. I don't find this statement credible. When I said that I did not agree with the return policy, I only said that the return should be selective. Within that context, it would not have been good for the town of Knin, and I still think the same, that among the returnees were the ring -- ring leaders of the rebellion against the Republic of Croatia. According to me, those who were allowed to return should have been those who had left and whose family members had stayed behind in the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So it's your view that only the Serbs who had family members who had stayed behind in Knin should be allowed to return to Knin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only them. I said that the approach should have been selective, which means when one group returned, and those were people who had family members and property in Knin, after that, applying a selective approach, all those who had return -- who had left would have been allowed to return.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, just to be clear, where it says in this memo that you disagreed with the policy regarding the return of those who left the area, as expressed recently by Mr. Kostovic, is your position that you never said that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the fact that, immediately after Operation Storm, those who had committed crimes and who had chased Croats from Knin should not return; for example, Babic, Martic and some other of the kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do not think that Ms. Gustafson is asking specifically on the return of Mr. Babic or Mr. Martic. But what she asked you is that what Mr. Al-Alfi reports you as having said - that is, to disagree with the policy - she asked you whether you deny that you ever said what is reported here as what you would have said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not deny this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please further explore, Ms. Gustafson, because I'm a bit --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in doubt.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So is this memo then correct, Mr. Pasic, that on the 12th of October you said to Mr. Al-Alfi that you disagreed with the policy regarding the return of those who left the area, as expressed recently by Mr. Kostovic? Did you say that to Mr. Al-Alfi on the 12th of October, 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not interested in exploring this any further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm looking at the clock, Ms. Gustafson. Could you give us an indication as --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think I need about another 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Another 15 minutes. Then we will have a break. But I would like to seek clarification on one issue and -- Mr. Pasic, we earlier spoke about the 56 sheep of your uncle. You remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, were you present when your uncle found out that his sheep had disappeared?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether I was present? Yes, I was in his house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you remember the time of the day when this happened? That he couldn't find his sheep anymore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I told you already, I think it was between 4.00 and 5.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said you advised him to report this to the police. Did you do that immediately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the disappearance of the sheep, I personally took him to the police station in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that on the same day or was that after hours, after a day, after two or three days? Could you tell us when you actually went to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same day, given that the distance between Knin and my village is 15 kilometres. Therefore, I believe we were at the police station in Knin by 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever return to the police station, in relation to the same matter? Or did you go once with your uncle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not. I simply drove him there, but I did not enter the police station building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know whether your uncle went ever back on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think he did. Had he wanted to go back, it would -- it would probably have to be me who would have taken him there. I don't think he had any other means of getting there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you take him back to your village after you had been to the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the only person who could bring him back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's what you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could you try to remember when you told Mr. Cermak about this uncle being robbed of his sheep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot recall exactly. I suppose, though, that while the uncle was in the police station, that I informed Mr. Cermak about the event during that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that would not be after a couple of hours, but you said you'd arrived at approximately 6.00 and then you went on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6.30. General Cermak was probably already aware of that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why do you think he was already aware of that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told him after you had taken your uncle to the police station or before you had taken your uncle to the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said already, it was while the uncle was talking to the police, reporting the missing sheep, I informed Mr. Cermak. I recall what I told him. I told him, General, there's no more lamb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you talk about the televisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you talk about the televisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, the next day, after I had been told that the TV sets were gone as well. It is then that I discussed it with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who told you that the TV sets were gone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The uncle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you then back in your village, or did you stay there overnight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't spend the night in the village but in Knin itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you then see or speak to your uncle again the next day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was not on duty and during my resting hours later in the afternoon, it is then that I would go to visit the uncle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you did not go with him to the police again, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you went to the police twice; first, on the day when the sheep had disappeared, and then on the next day again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Only when the sheep disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When were the -- was the robbery of the television sets then ever reported to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not. When did you become aware of the possible perpetrators to have been found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know the names of the perpetrators, nor did I know when they were found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have a break, but I will first invite Madam Usher to escort you. We have a break of some 25 minutes. Could you please follow Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties may have wondered about my last few questions to the witness on reporting. The reason why I did it, and I think it is appropriate that the parties should be aware of that, is that, Ms. Gustafson, you rely upon the statement of Mr. Cermak and reporting back the theft of some sheep to, among others, Mr. Cermak. Whereas, you, Mr. Kay, you rely on where Mr. Luka Pasic reports to the police the theft of these sheep. Well, first of all, I noticed that, from the television sets, I do not read one word about that. However, I noticed that the report to the police by Mr. Luka Pasic, at least the document you submitted, Mr. Kay, talks about Mr. Luka Pasic reporting on the 20th of October, at a quarter to 4.00 in the afternoon, the theft of his sheep. Whereas, we find in this -- we also find in -- I think it is also in 2645, that, already, at 3.00 on that day, persons were found, persons who later then were detained in relation to this matter. We also find in the reports that, on the 19th, the theft was established at 5.00 or 5.30 in the afternoon, which means that, at least I have some difficulties, in view of the inconsistencies also in view of what the witness just answered to my questions, to gain a better insight in what actually happened. That is, was it the phone call, even before Mr. Pasic had reported to the police on the 20th of October at 3.45 p.m., that had triggered the police activity; or was it, as the witness just told us, a reporting already on the evening of the theft, that is, the 19th of October, which certainly finds no confirmation in the report. That's the reason why I tried to seek further information about what is a matter on which the parties apparently take a different starting point in considering what triggered the police activity. We will have a break, and we'll resume at ten minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, in your statement to -- that you gave to the Defence, you said that there was no Croatian government or local authorities' plan to expel Serbs and move in the Croats instead. And that's at paragraph 29. And I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about that conclusion. In your Prosecution statement at page 2, you said you had no knowledge of the coming of Operation Storm. So I take it from that, that you were not involved in the planning of Operation Storm, and you were not informed about the plans for Operation Storm. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you didn't attend any meetings with President Tudjman when plans regarding -- or policies regarding the Krajina Serbs or the movement of Croats into the Krajina were discussed, were you? Or did you attend any such meetings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But there was a policy, was there not, to move Croats into the homes that had been vacated by the Serbs who had left the Krajina during or after Operation Storm, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Pasic, your -- your statement to the Prosecution says that you received instructions from Mr. Radic, the minister for reconstruction and development, to move -- to house returning Croats in Knin, and that Knin itself was soon very full. You've given evidence today that Croats were moved into Knin from other places, such as -- who had come from other places, such as Bosnia. And you also gave evidence today that after Operation Storm, the demographic picture in Knin was reversed, and it was about 90 per cent Croat. Can -- how do you reconcile that evidence with your statement that there was no policy to move Croats into the houses that had been vacated by Serbs who had left the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still stand by the opinion that there was no policy of expelling Serbs and bringing in Croats in their stead. Croats, at least some of them, were, in a way, forced to move into Knin. After Operation Storm, a great many Serbs arrived in Banja Luka. With their arrival there, they simply told the Croats there in their own flats, This is where I'm going stay from now on and you take my house or my flat over there. So it was not a planned thing. That is one thing. Another thing, as for the movement of Croats from other parts of Croatia into the Krajina was an expression of their wish to deal with their housing problem. They wanted to settle in the town of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the housing commission in Knin and Minister Radic facilitated those wishes of Croats to move into Knin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move to something else that you said in your Defence statement at paragraph 27, which was that -- you stated that the ECMM requested that civilian police patrols be cancelled because the Serbs did not trust the civilian police and that the patrols were withdrawn. And you stated that the ECMM representatives were supposed to protect them - and I -- I take that to be a reference to civilians - but they did not protect them. Now, the Chamber has received substantial evidence from ECMM monitors and ECMM reports, and there's no indication from any of that evidence that the ECMM ever requested civilian police patrols to be cancelled. So I'd like to ask you what exactly is the source of your information that the ECMM requested civilian police patrols to be cancelled?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source was the ECMM itself, as well as the inhabitants who informed them of those wishes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And how did you learn of this information from the ECMM? Who told you that the ECMM had requested police patrols to be cancelled?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, in Knin itself, there may have been some ten different organisations and types of monitors. I couldn't tell them apart, but I can tell you decidedly that in the discussions with them, they expressed their wish for the Croatian police not to enter certain villages. They said that they were going to protect those villages, which they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I take it from your answer that you can't remember which particular organisation or which particular person gave you this information, about wanting police patrols to be cancelled?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but I know it came from them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we look at P953, please. And, Your Honour, I'd like to tender 65 ter 2353, which was the 12th of October memo from Mr. Al-Alfi, which I forgot to do before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 02353 becomes Exhibit P2648.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Pasic, I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 1 of this report, which starts with the words, "General situation ..." And this is a report from the 9th of October, 1995. It's a daily report from Team Knin of the ECMM. And it says: "The stronger CRO police patrolling," and that's a reference to Croatian police, "after the Varivode massacre seems to improve the security situation. However, little is left to protect and it is clear that this new policy is the result of international pressure, rather than it was a planned move. Why did we need a Varivode and why did it come so late? Small-scale looting is still going on." Now, here, Mr. Pasic, the ECMM is observing increased police patrols, has improved the situation, and is asking why it is happening so late. If it is the fact, as you suggest, that the ECMM had requested the Croatian police not to patrol, why would they have written this report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the crime in Varivode and in Gosici, Croatian police patrols became more frequent, irrespective of the fact that some wanted to see them reduced. This is what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right. But, Mr. Pasic, your evidence is that the ECMM didn't want the Croatian police to patrol. This is an ECMM report. If the ECMM didn't want the police -- Croatian police to patrol, why does it say that patrolling has improved the situation and ask why it is happening so late? Why doesn't it say, Croatian police are patrolling and we don't want them to patrol? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, in certain areas were designated as those in which patrols were not welcome. That is to say, in certain areas where more civilians remained after Operation Storm, it is actually good that there was patrolling there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to something else now, which is -- relates to something you said on Thursday in your evidence. And you said that you were -- in response to a question by Mr. Misetic, you said that you were certain that around the 18th of August, the 4th and 7th Guards Brigades were not involved in any burning or looting. And you said: "I toured the settlements around Knin, and it was said that this was not done by the members of the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade." Now, I'd like to ask you: Which specific settlements did you go to; and who specifically did you speak to; and what specifically did they say to you about the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had gone and I had often visited my village. I was in Plavno, Podkonje, but there were no Serbs left there, only Croats. I was in -- in Biskupija, in Ocestovo. I don't know how many villages I visited. I also went to Vidosevci, to Macure, which is also part of Kistanje. I visited a number of settlements and villages that belonged to the municipal area of the city of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And who specifically did you speak to who told you that looting and burning was not done by members of the 4th and 7th Guards Brigades?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was with people who remained living in their houses after Operation Storm. If I were to tell you now that in Kistanje, the gentleman's name was Djuro Macura, that in Plavno I spoke to Ilica Torbica. In Ocestovo, I spoke to Rade Tango. In my own village I spoke to my uncle, and everybody else who lived there, I don't know whether that would be enough. What else can I tell you?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand, Mr. Pasic, specific information you received from these people that you spoke to about the 4th and 7th Guards Brigades. Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: What specifically did these people tell you; and if could you tell me, who, where, when, and what they told you about the 4th and 7th Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they arrived, members who borne the insignia of the brigades, and people are literate and they could understand those insignia, those people told them, Stay in your houses, nobody will touch you, you are going to be safe there, you can rest assured that you will not be touched.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You've told me the what. Now I'd like the who, and the when, and the where.

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to Mile Kovacevic in the village of Oton and Brdo. I can't remember all of their names, but I know what they told me. If I may add to that, I just remembered, I spoke to a gentleman from Orlic in the Biskupija territory. His name was Nikola Tica. He remained living there, and I believe that members of the 4th Guards Brigade paid him a visit on somebody's instructions, but I don't know whose instructions those were.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you remember when either of these conversations took place?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 15 years ago. I did not pay too much attention to all that. It would be pure speculation if I gave you a specific time or date.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go back to -- to the subject that we were speaking about on -- in your evidence on Friday, which was the changes that you made to your statements, and I have one more question I'd like to ask you about that. And you remember His Honour Judge Orie was asking you some questions about last weekend, when you read your statements over several times and found mistakes in them. And at transcript page 22818, Judge Orie said to you: "Then you read your statements on Friday evening and found that there was still a lot of inaccuracies. Then you met the next morning with Mr. Basic, and after had you met with him, you, as you said, read your statements again. You read them over several times. Is that finding, again, that they were not in every respect true and correct? Is that a fair summary of what you told us?" And your answer was: "The moment I realised that my statements would used before this Tribunal, my opinion changed completely." And the Judge asked you: "Your opinion about what?" And you said: "My opinion of the statements that had been given and that did not contain elements of what I had said and did contain certain statements that I had given without much thought, because I did not believe that they would be used anywhere and at any point in time." Now, my question is, when you told His Honour Judge Orie that you realised your statements would be used before the Tribunal last weekend and then your opinion of your statements changed completely, and your statements contained comments that you had given without much thought, my question is: When you came to The Hague on Tuesday, did you change -- did you make changes to any of those comments, comments that you had given without much thought?

utterances.speaker: PETAR PASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And I also said on Friday that if I were to be asked to do the same thing tomorrow, I would make corrections in some other statements as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
